{{Short description|Type of matrix in linear algebra}}
In [[linear algebra]], a [[square matrix|square]] [[nonnegative matrix]] <math> A </math> of order <math> n </math> is said to be '''productive''', or to be a '''Leontief matrix''', if there exists a <math>  n \times 1 </math> nonnegative [[column matrix]] <math> P </math>  such as <math> P-AP </math> is a [[positive matrix]].

==History==

The concept of productive matrix was developed by the economist [[Wassily Leontief]] ([[Nobel Prize in Economics]] in 1973) in order to model and analyze the relations between the different sectors of an economy.<ref>Kim Minju, [http://www.unc.edu/~marzuola/Math547_S13/Math547_S13_Projects/M_Kim_Section001_Leontief_IO_Model.pdf Leontief Input-Output Model (Application of Linear Algebra to Economics)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141215221356/http://www.unc.edu/~marzuola/Math547_S13/Math547_S13_Projects/M_Kim_Section001_Leontief_IO_Model.pdf# |date=2014-12-15 }}</ref> The interdependency linkages between the latter can be examined by the [[input-output model]] with empirical data.

==Explicit definition==

The matrix <math>A\in\mathrm{M}_{n,n}(\R)</math> is productive if and only if <math> A \geqslant 0 </math> and <math> \exists P \in\mathrm{M}_{n,1}(\R), P>0</math> such as <math>P-AP>0</math>.

Here <math>\mathrm{M}_{r,c}(\R)</math> denotes the [[Matrix_(mathematics)#Notation|set of ''r''×''c'' matrices]] of [[real number]]s, whereas <math> >0</math> and <math>\geqslant 0</math> indicates a positive and a [[nonnegative matrix]], respectively.

==Properties==
The following properties are proven e.g. in the textbook (Michel 1984).<ref>[[Philippe Michel (economist)|Philippe Michel]], "9.2 Matrices productives", ''Cours de Mathématiques pour Economistes'', Édition Economica, 1984</ref>

===Characterization===
'''Theorem'''
A nonnegative matrix <math>A\in\mathrm{M}_{n,n}(\R)</math> is productive if and only if <math>I_n - A</math> is [[invertible matrix|invertible]] with a nonnegative inverse, where <math>I_n</math> denotes the <math>n \times n</math> [[identity matrix]].

'''Proof'''

"If" :
:Let <math>I_n-A</math> be invertible with a nonnegative inverse,
:Let <math>U \in\mathrm{M}_{n,1}(\R)</math> be an arbitrary column matrix with <math>U>0</math>.
:Then the matrix <math>P = (I_n - A)^{-1}U</math> is nonnegative since it is the product of two nonnegative matrices.
:Moreover, <math>P - AP = (I_n - A) P = (I_n - A) (I_n - A)^{-1} U = U > 0</math>.
:Therefore <math>A</math> is productive.
"Only if" :
:Let <math>A</math> be productive, let <math>P > 0</math> such that <math>V = P - AP > 0</math>.
:The proof proceeds by ''[[reductio ad absurdum]]''. 
:First, assume for contradiction <math>I_n - A</math> is [[singular matrix|singular]].
::The [[endomorphism]] canonically associated with <math>I_n - A</math> can not be [[injective]] by singularity of the matrix.
::Thus some non-zero column matrix <math>Z\in\mathrm{M}_{n,1}(\R)</math> exists such that <math>(I_n - A) Z = 0</math>.
::The matrix <math>-Z</math> has the same properties as <math>Z</math>, therefore we can choose <math>Z</math> as an element of the [[kernel (algebra)|kernel]] with at least one positive entry.
::Hence <math>c = \sup_{i \in [|1,n|]}\frac{z_i}{p_i}</math> is nonnegative and reached with at least one value <math>k \in [|1,n|]</math>.
::By definition of <math>V</math> and of <math>Z</math>, we can infer that:
:::<math>cv_k = c (p_k - \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}p_i) = cp_k -  \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}cp_i</math>
:::<math>cp_k = z_k = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}z_i</math>, using that <math>Z = AZ</math> by construction.
::Thus <math> cv_k = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki} (z_i - cp_i) \leq\ 0</math>, using that <math>z_i \leq cp_i</math> by definition of <math>c</math>.
::This contradicts <math>c > 0</math> and <math>v_k > 0</math>, hence <math>I_n - A</math> is necessarily invertible.
:Second, assume for contradiction <math>I_n - A</math> is invertible but with at least one negative entry in its inverse.
::Hence <math>\exists X \in\mathrm{M}_{n,1}(\R), X  \geqslant 0</math> such that there is at least one negative entry in <math>Y = (I_n - A)^{-1} X</math>.
::Then <math>c = \sup_{i \in [|1,n|]}-\frac{y_i}{p_i}</math> is positive and reached with at least one value <math>k \in [|1,n|]</math>.
::By definition of <math>V</math> and of <math>X</math>, we can infer that:
:::<math>cv_k = c (p_k - \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}p_i) = -y_k  -\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}cp_i</math>
:::<math>x_k = y_k - \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki}y_i</math>, using that <math>X = (I_n-A)Y</math> by construction
:::<math>cv_k + x_k = - \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ki} (cp_i + y_i) \geqslant 0</math> using that <math>-y_i \leqslant cp_i</math> by definition of <math>c</math>.
::Thus <math>x_k \leq - cv_k < 0</math>, contradicting <math>X \geqslant 0</math>.
::Therefore <math>(I_n - A)^{-1}</math> is necessarily nonnegative.

===Transposition===
'''Proposition'''
The [[transpose]] of a productive matrix is productive.

'''Proof'''

:Let <math>A\in\mathrm{M}_{n,n}(\R)</math> a productive matrix.
:Then <math>(I_n - A)^{-1}</math> exists and is nonnegative.
:Yet <math>(I_n - A^T)^{-1} = ((I_n - A)^T)^{-1} = ((I_n - A)^{-1})^T</math>
:Hence <math>(I_n - A^T)</math> is invertible with a nonnegative inverse.
:Therefore <math>A^T</math> is productive.

==Application==

{{Main article|Input-output analysis}}

With a matrix approach of the [[input-output model]], the consumption matrix is productive if it is economically  viable and if the latter and the demand vector are nonnegative.
